articles.title: Will the Zuckerberg, Musk and Altman movies make a dent on tech giant evangelism?
articles.summary: The triple release of The Social Reckoning, Musk and Artificial is less a clear political stance, more like movie studio opportunism. Hollywood is sending a clear message: it’s a friend of tech.
body: The enormous pull of the tech industry – including its many trillions of dollars, oversized influence on politics and heavily pushed algorithms and AI products – means Hollywood is not alone in courting its wealth, but it has intensified the historic tension between art and commerce in the entertainment business. Technology that augments the human experience may be a compelling narrative subject, but this year brings a trio of films about the gurus responsible for the industry’s false promises.

Time will tell how severely these films will affect the credibility of their subjects, but recent surveys indicate young Americans are already turning on giants such as Zuckerberg, Musk, and Altman. It seems as if these projects are taking advantage of a rising tide of tech scepticism rather than forging it themselves. What’s more noteworthy is how the films coincide with the widespread devaluing of films as art by corporations and their products.
points: The triple release of The Social Reckoning, Musk and Artificial is less a clear political stance, more like movie studio opportunism.
Hollywood is sending a clear message: it’s a friend of tech.

body: After playing a junkie who breaks into a house and stumbles upon 17 missing children in “Weapons,” Abrams teamed up again with director Zach Cregger, this time as the lead of “Resident Evil.” Instead of playing one of the video game series’ gun-toting protagonists, Abrams stars as a medical courier tasked with delivering a mysterious package to a zombie-infested city. And shortly after “Resident Evil,” he headed to an even more dangerous location: the belly of a whale. Yes, Abrams is reuniting with his “Weapons” co-star Josh Brolin in “Whalefall,” a survival thriller about a scuba diver who gets swallowed whole by a giant sperm whale.

articles.title: Post your questions for Celia Imrie
articles.summary: From Miss Babs in Acorn Antiques to Calendar Girls, The Best Exotic Marigold Hotel and her infamous appearance on The Celebrity Traitors, it’s hard to know where to begin. Celia Imrie has had such a varied career, it’s hard to know where you might know her best from.
body: Maybe you know her as Mrs Quickly, the ghastly would-be stepmother in Nanny McPhee. Or maybe you first encountered her in Upstairs, Downstairs, To the Manor Born, Bergerac, Lovejoy or The Darling Buds of May, or as Claudia Bing, the magnificently awful PR rival of Jennifer Saunders’ Edina in Absolutely Fabulous.

More recently, she returned as Una in Bridget Jones: Mad About the Boy; joined Helen Mirren, Pierce Brosnan and Ben Kingsley in The Thursday Murder Club; and popped up in The Diplomat. Then, of course, there was The Celebrity Traitors. Imrie entered the castle as a Faithful, survived being chained up in a wooden cabin, and accidentally farted while doing so – instantly producing the Guardian’s No 2 TV moment of the year – and eventually got murdered in plain sight by Alan Carr.

Now she’s back as in (yes, it’s nearly that time already) Merry Christmas Aubrey Flint, alongside John Bradley as a Christmas-hating model-soldier painter sentenced to community service at a struggling retirement home, where he somehow ends up directing a chaotic production of A Christmas Carol. Richard E Grant and Jim Broadbent are along for the festive ride, too.

articles.title: The Social Reckoning review – Aaron Sorkin’s jittery sequel with all-new evil puppet Zuckerberg
articles.summary: Jeremy Strong’s slow-talking Facebook founder turns into a cameo, background to a thriller about a whistleblower that somehow never mentions Trump. Here is a film for all those people who solemnly deplore social media in conversation but haven’t quite got round to deleting their accounts.
body: Zuckerberg, though, is almost a cameo, with no equals with whom he can exchange dialogue, only employees – although the film imagines one former investor-turned-critic called Charlie (Bill Burr) who heckles Zuckerberg’s practice performance before a confessional hearing, with Zuckerberg amusingly having to be told how to smile. Charlie is the angry, unheeded voice of conscience.

The resulting drama rattles along at an entertaining clip, although there are false notes. When Frances has secret meetings with Horwitz in a hotel, the film has her wearing a slinky evening dress, supposedly as a kind of disguise, so that if recognised it would seem like she was out on a date. Hmm, really? Or is it so that the movie’s female lead has scenes where she looks glamorous? Later, Horwitz affectionately tells her to be less “mean”. But she is not “mean”. She just speaks Sorkinspeak. So does Horwitz. The ubiquity of Sorkinspeak effaces the difference between all the characters.
points: Jeremy Strong’s slow-talking Facebook founder turns into a cameo, background to a thriller about a whistleblower that somehow never mentions Trump.

articles.title: King Charles and Elton John in the audience for Apple music workshop
articles.summary: Charles and Sir Elton visit an Apple x King's Trust Creative Labs music event offering industry skills to young people.
body: King Charles has visited a hi-tech music workshop for young people, in a collaboration between his King's Trust charity and technology firm Apple.
Pop royalty, in the form of Sir Elton John, was a special guest at the event, sitting beside the King, as they listened to a short performance from singer-songwriter Skye Newman.
The event was held at a music hall in Apple's headquarters building, in the restored Battersea Power Station in south west London.
The project being backed by the King is intended to equip young people with practical skills to work in the creative industries.

articles.title: Ari Emanuel Opens a Can of Worms… And Eats Them Every Morning
articles.summary: The super-agent’s new memoir spills plenty of Hollywood tea. But his breakfast ritual, which includes a heaping cup of parasitic helminths, is definitely hard to swallow.
body: There are tons of eyebrow-raising revelations in Ari Emanuel ’s recently released memoir, Roll the Calls. Like how he secretly fed Nikki Finke damaging leaks to help engineer his 2009 takeover of William Morris. Or how he believes Jeffrey Katzenberg helped cover up President Joe Biden’s mental decline. Or how Larry David and Elon Musk nearly came to blows at Emanuel’s 2022 wedding.

“Upon waking,” Emanuel writes on page 232, describing his personal prescription for a healthy morning ritual, “drink two bottles of mineral water, do 40 minutes of stretching, do 10 minutes of dynamic warm-ups, do a regimen of extremely difficult breath work, then dive into the sauna, then 20 minutes of meditation, then 10 minutes in the ice plunge, then 20 minutes of infrared light therapy, then a protein shake with coffee and vitamins, topped off with a cup of live worms.”
points: The super-agent’s new memoir spills plenty of Hollywood tea.
But his breakfast ritual, which includes a heaping cup of parasitic helminths, is definitely hard to swallow.

articles.title: Long Live Steve McQueen: Why the King of Cool Is Hot Again
articles.summary: Three reboots of signature McQueen movies — ‘The Thomas Crown Affair,’ ‘Bullitt,’ and ‘The Getaway’ — are currently in the works. Says his grandkid, “Cool never expires.”
body: Steve McQueen has been dead for 46 years, yet somehow he’s juggling one of the busiest development slates in town. At the moment, three of his signature movies are simultaneously being resurrected — one by another famous Steven, as in Spielberg — while a fourth project based on an ex-wife’s memoir continues to gestate as either a possible drama or documentary.

Meanwhile, Adolescence director Philip Barantini is attached to a Netflix remake of The Getaway, the 1972 Sam Peckinpah bank robbery drama on which McQueen met future wife Ali MacGraw. No cast has been announced. And at Amblin, Spielberg is developing a movie based on McQueen’s character in the 1968 cop drama Bullitt — not a remake so much as a new storyline about the San Francisco detective. Bradley Cooper is said to be attached to star.

articles.title: Xbox bets on Gears of War in battle of gaming giants
articles.summary: Unlike other flagship titles, E-Day will only be available on Xbox at a time of rising console costs.
body: Gears of War, one of the video games that helped Microsoft's Xbox to win over millions of fans, is back.
Prequel E-Day takes players back to where it all started, telling the origin story of humanity's conflict with The Locust - the series' horrifying enemy species.
The game's been well-received by critics and players, but it's also seen as a big test of Xbox's new direction.
Unlike recent flagship titles from the company's studios, which have been released on PlayStation 5 and, in some cases, Nintendo Switch, E-Day is being pushed as an Xbox exclusive.
